analysis.one_liner: Lets states pool federal health program money into one state-run universal coverage plan.
analysis.headline: Introduced in July 2025 and sent to five House committees, the bill has had no hearings, markups, or votes; 35 Democrats back it and no Republican has signed on.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill writes a new section into the Affordable Care Act letting any state apply to combine the federal money it now receives for Medicare, Medicaid, CHIP, ACA subsidies, federal employee coverage, and military health coverage into one publicly run state health plan. A state would have to cover at least 95% of its residents within five years, keep the plan affordable, and show a ten-year budget that costs the federal government no more than it spends today. The plan must cover everyone in the state, including benefits for reproductive health, contraception, and gender-affirming care, and people could still buy extra private insurance on top of it.
analysis.who_benefits: Residents of any state that opts in: the roughly uninsured, people buying subsidized marketplace plans, and families squeezed by out-of-pocket costs would get a single public plan with comprehensive benefits and cost-sharing protections at least as strong as what they have now. People with employer coverage, Medicaid, or federal coverage would be folded into one plan with no premiums or cost-sharing above what the state plan sets.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Residents of states that opt in

how_it_helps.text: A state plan must cover every resident of the state, including those currently on Medicaid, CHIP, marketplace plans, federal employee coverage, and TRICARE, with coverage at least as comprehensive and cost-sharing at least as affordable as the federal programs it replaces.

The plan must be publicly administered by a state agency or independent public entity, and states must reach coverage for at least 95% of residents within five years or risk losing the waiver after a grace period.

Federal money that would have been spent on those programs in the state—including premium tax credits and Medicaid payments, adjusted for caseload growth and medical inflation—is paid to the state instead, and any savings can be reinvested in health services.

The state plan must include coverage for reproductive health care, including abortion, contraception, and gender-affirming care, and residents keep the right to buy supplemental private insurance for benefits the plan doesn't cover.

States must hold public hearings and submit an independent five-year report on coverage, affordability, and quality, with federal technical assistance and possible waiver termination if the state misses the coverage target.

analysis.who_pays: If a state opts in, the bill requires the arrangement to be budget-neutral for the federal government, so the remaining cost of universal coverage falls on the state, which would have to raise it through its own taxes or other financing. Private insurers in that state lose the main coverage business, and employers would face whatever state financing the plan's law imposes.
analysis.who_pays_short: State budgets, then insurers and employers

drawbacks.text: The bill requires a ten-fiscal-year plan that is budget-neutral for the federal government, so any gap between pooled federal funds and the cost of covering everyone must be financed by the state—a cost that could run to billions a year and require new state taxes.

The waiver would fold Medicare, TRICARE, and federal employee coverage for state residents into a state-run plan, a major restructuring that could disrupt benefits and networks people currently rely on, even if the bill requires the new coverage to be at least as comprehensive.

Only states that choose to apply get the benefit, so coverage gains depend entirely on state politics; a state that opts in and then misses the 95% coverage target after a 12-month grace period can have its waiver terminated.

The plan must cover abortion, contraception, and gender-affirming care for all residents, which guarantees legal and political challenges in conservative states and makes the framework a likely flashpoint.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For a state willing to finance it, the bill offers a genuine path to near-universal coverage with strong consumer protections, public reporting, and an escape valve for poorly performing states. The serious costs are honest ones: the state must make up the financing gap, the transition would be the largest health-system restructuring any state has attempted, and residents currently satisfied with their Medicare or employer coverage would be moved into a new system. Whether the trade is worth it would be decided state by state.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to five House committees on the same day, and in the months since it has received no hearings, no markup, and no floor action, so it is still waiting on committee chairs to move it.

narrative.text: Rep. Ro Khanna introduced the State-Based Universal Health Care Act of 2025 on July 15, 2025, joined by 23 original cosponsors.

The same day, the bill was referred to five committees—Energy and Commerce, Armed Services, Ways and Means, Oversight and Government Reform, and Education and Workforce—for consideration of the parts under each panel's jurisdiction.
The bill has since accrued 35 cosponsors, all of them Democrats, with no Republican support recorded.
The action history shows no activity after the initial referrals—no hearings, no committee votes, and no floor action.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because nothing has happened, the state of play benefits opponents of a state universal-coverage option: private insurers keep their current market, and no state can yet opt out of the fragmented system. Supporters keep a live bill but no votes are scheduled.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Insurers and the status quo, for now

for.name: Rep. Ro Khanna
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to let states pool federal health program funding into a universal state plan.

for.name: 35 House cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Signed on in support, all from the Democratic caucus; none from the Republican side.

against.name: Chairs of the five referred committees (Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, Armed Services, Oversight, Education and Workforce)
against.what_they_did: Have not scheduled hearings or markups on the bill since its July 2025 referral, leaving it without any action beyond referral.

sides.party_line_note: All 35 cosponsors are Democrats and the bill's sponsor is a Democrat; no Republican has signed on, and with Republicans holding the House majority the committees that would move the bill are chaired by the opposing party.

industries.note: In any state that opts in, the main business of selling or administering Medicaid managed care, marketplace plans, Medicare Advantage, and employer coverage would be replaced by a publicly administered state plan. Insurers could still sell supplemental coverage for benefits the plan doesn't offer, but their core role would shrink drastically.

The bill lets a state waive the federal employer mandate and ERISA preemption for plan years in the waiver, so employers in an opting state would face whatever financing and rules the state's plan law sets instead. Some employer obligations would end, but states would likely look to employers to help fund universal coverage.

Universal coverage in an opting state would sharply cut uncompensated care, a chronic financial strain on hospitals, but a single public payer typically pays lower rates than private insurance. The bill requires any savings to be reinvested in health services.

analysis.trajectory: The bill sits with five committees and no scheduled action months after referral. Single-party sponsorship, no Republican cosponsors, and a Republican House majority make a floor vote unlikely this Congress; the realistic path is that the bill goes nowhere unless a state-focused coalition builds bipartisan support or a future majority revives it.
